name: Guinea-Bissau
card_headline: The junta's 12-month transition ends on 26 November with no election date, after officials said the 6 December vote cannot happen.
card_summary: Soldiers seized power on 26 November 2025, a day before results of a disputed election. Maj.-Gen. Horta Inta-a leads a transition meant to end with elections on 6 December 2026. On 8 October the prime minister and the electoral commission said the conditions are not met, and no new date has been set. A new constitution approved in August expands presidential powers. Cocaine trafficking, a one-crop economy and cuts in food aid frame the stakes.
card_local: O Democrata in Bissau reports that the Transition Council judged the 6 December vote unworkable and that a presidential decree on a new date was still pending on 25 October. [1][2]
card_international: Reuters and AFP report that the prime minister and the electoral commission said the conditions for the 6 December vote are not met, and Lusa reports no new date as the transition term ends on 26 November. [3][4][5]
card_scholar: GI-TOC found in August 2025 that the cocaine market was booming again, and the World Bank's June 2026 update says growth rests on a single crop. [6][7]
context_md: Guinea-Bissau has had five coups and numerous attempted takeovers since independence from Portugal in 1974. [4] The UN describes it as a gateway for Latin American drugs bound for Europe. [8] Incumbent Umaro Sissoco Embalo and challenger Fernando Dias both claimed victory in the 23 November 2025 vote. [9] Soldiers seized power on 26 November, before results were published, and Maj.-Gen. Horta Inta-a was sworn in as transitional president on 27 November. [10] The country is suspended from the African Union, ECOWAS and the CPLP. [5] The economy depends heavily on cashew exports. [9]

sections.title: The transition ends on 26 November without an election date
sections.body_md:
Soldiers appeared on state television on 26 November 2025 and said they had taken power, a day before the electoral commission was due to publish provisional results from the 23 November vote. [11][9] The commission later said armed men had seized ballots, tally sheets and computers and destroyed the results server, so the count cannot be completed. [10] Major-General Horta Inta-a (also spelled N'Tam and N'Ta) was sworn in on 27 November for a one-year transition. [10]

The charter published in early December bars the interim president and the prime minister from standing and creates a 65-member National Transition Council. [12] In January Inta-a set presidential and legislative elections for 6 December 2026. [13] On 8 October Prime Minister Ilidio Vieira Te told reporters the vote must be postponed: parties had not held the congresses needed to choose leaders, and potential candidates had missed the 6 October deadline to file with the Supreme Court. [3] Electoral commission official Felisberta Moura Vaz said the commission had told Inta-a the conditions were not met, and called the date a matter for the transitional president. [4] On 9 October the Transition Council's spokesperson said the procedural steps required by electoral law were practically compromised. The council proposed no new date. [1]

Lusa reports that no new date exists as the 12 months run out. On 6 November the military council said parties could hold meetings from 24 November, while rallies and demonstrations stay banned. [5] PAIGC leader Domingos Simoes Pereira told a Portuguese parliamentary committee on 6 October that political activity is suspended and that he knew of no candidacy filed. He has been in Portugal since 24 July, after detention from 10 July in a case over an alleged October 2025 coup plot. [14] Embalo said in late September he would run, and the military high command refused his return in early October, citing security. [15]

lenses.local: O Democrata reports that the Transition Council called the December vote unworkable and that the government and the commission acknowledged it cannot be held, with a presidential decree on a new date still pending on 25 October. [1][2]
lenses.international: Reuters, AFP and Lusa carry the postponement, the missed candidacy deadline and the absence of a new date. [3][4][5]
lenses.scholar: International IDEA's democracy tracker records the December 2025 charter and its bar on the interim president and prime minister standing. [12]

sections.title: A contested coup, a stronger presidency and a narrowing civic space
sections.body_md:
Opposition figures and several foreign voices say the November 2025 coup was staged to keep Embalo in power. Former Nigerian President Goodluck Jonathan, who led an observer mission, called it a "ceremonial coup", and Senegal's prime minister, Ousmane Sonko, called the takeover a scheme. Control Risks analyst Beverly Ochieng noted that one coup leader was Embalo's personal military adviser. [11] The soldiers said they foiled a plot involving politicians and a drug lord, which AP did not verify. [11] AFP reports that several presidential guard members were disarmed in late September, and that the new leadership has reportedly distanced itself from Embalo. [4]

The National Transition Council adopted a new constitution on 13 January, according to the UN Secretary-General's report. [16] Voters approved it on 30 August: the electoral commission reported about 70 percent in favour and turnout of almost 60 percent, while news agencies reported largely empty polling stations. The president can appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet and dissolve parliament under conditions, and seats fall from 102 to 65. The PAIGC called for a boycott. [17] Lusa adds that diaspora voters are barred from presidential elections, and the prime minister said in September he would lead a new party. [5]

After the coup the authorities banned demonstrations and press conferences, intimidated rights defenders and closed party offices, the UN Secretary-General reports. The body of youth movement leader Vigario Luis Balanta, reportedly beaten to death, was found on 31 March. [16] The government denies any role and says it is investigating. [3] RSF ranks the country 100th of 180 in its 2026 index, up from 110th, and says the junta suspended some outlets and banned coverage of opposition press conferences. [18] CPJ called in January for the authorities to rescind an order banning unauthorized press conferences. [19] The Guinean Human Rights League said on 3 November that five men have been held for over a year without judicial process, a claim carried by one outlet. [20]

lenses.local: O Democrata quotes PSTGB leader Sene Bacai Cassamá saying parties lack freedom to speak, and calling for elections within six months. [21]
lenses.international: AP carries the staged-coup allegations, and AFP and Reuters carried the referendum result and the empty polling stations. [11][17]
lenses.scholar: The ISS wrote in 2014, after an earlier coup, that elections alone would not resolve the root causes of instability. [22]

sections.title: Cocaine money sits behind the junta's justification and earlier killings
sections.body_md:
The soldiers said they acted against a plot by national drug lords, according to General Denis N'Canha, head of the presidential military office, quoted by AFP. [8] The UN describes the country as a gateway for Latin American drugs bound for Europe. A GI-TOC report from August 2025 found the cocaine market booming again and possibly more profitable than at any point in the country's history, with retail cocaine and crack prices falling. [8]

The same GI-TOC report puts wholesale prices in Bissau at 7,000 euros a kilogram, down from 10,000 to 16,000 euros, after a trafficker sold off stock. It describes the July 2025 killing of presidential guard member Tano Bari, and says the government suspended RTP and Agencia Lusa and expelled their journalists on 15 August 2025. [6] The Guinean Human Rights League still calls for accountability over Bari's death and Balanta's, and no official finding has been reported. [20] The Attorney General's Office has announced an inquiry commission into Balanta's death. [5]

Earlier cases show how traffickers and officials overlap. A US court sentenced a son of a former president to more than six years for leading a heroin-trafficking ring. [11] GI-TOC argued in 2022 that the political-military elite's role in the cocaine trade has driven cycles of instability. [23] RSF says journalists self-censor on drug trafficking, and many earn about 50 euros a month. [18] This draft found no 2026 seizure figures and no source on how the junta's drug claim has been tested.

lenses.local: Local reporting on drugs is thin in this draft: RSF says self-censorship is common on the subject and corruption gets little coverage. [18]
lenses.international: AFP and AP carry the junta's drug-plot claim and note that AP did not verify it. [8][11]
lenses.scholar: GI-TOC's August 2025 report links cocaine money to campaign finance and says the Judicial Police's capacity to investigate is limited. [6]

sections.title: ECOWAS rejected the plan, then handed the file to Senegal
sections.body_md:
ECOWAS heads of state met in Abuja on 14 December 2025 and rejected the junta's transition plan. They asked for a short, inclusive transition and threatened targeted sanctions on those obstructing it. [24] A mission led by Sierra Leone's President Julius Maada Bio, who chairs the bloc, and Senegal's President Bassirou Diomaye Faye met the military leaders and demanded the release of detained opponents, including Pereira. [13] The UN Secretary-General's report says Pereira was released to house arrest on 30 January through Senegal's defence minister, and that ECOWAS welcomed proposals for an inclusive government that the opposition rejected as made without consultation. [16]

The ECOWAS summit in Lungi, Sierra Leone, on 19 July named Senegal facilitator of the transition. [25] It also urged the unconditional release of detained political figures. [26] Senegal's foreign minister, Cheikh Niang, returned to Bissau on 25 October to discuss a new election date and to meet parties, including the PAIGC and its dissidents, MADEM-G15 and the PRS. [2][27] Cassamá of the PSTGB said the ECOWAS mission left without clear outcomes and consulted a restricted group. [21]

Bissau also pursues a UN Security Council seat for 2028 and 2029, which the prime minister confirmed at the General Assembly on 25 September. The Assembly vote is scheduled for June 2027, and a candidate needs two-thirds of votes cast. [28]

lenses.local: O Democrata reports Niang's October agenda and the PSTGB leader's criticism that ECOWAS met only a narrow group. [2][21]
lenses.international: Reuters carried ECOWAS's rejection and sanctions warning, and Xinhua and Africanews carried the Senegal mandate. [24][25][26]
lenses.scholar: The ISS wrote in 2014 that ECOWAS was the most influential outside actor in the earlier transition and that a new coup would damage its credibility. [22]

sections.title: Growth of 5.8 percent rests on cashew, while debt, hunger and a vaccine-trial row weigh
sections.body_md:
The IMF estimates growth of about 5.8 percent in 2025, driven by agriculture, especially cashew exports, and expects a slowdown in 2026. [29] The World Bank's June update projects 4.8 percent for 2026 and reports inflation of 0.9 percent in 2025, a fiscal deficit of 6.5 percent of GDP and public debt of 75.6 percent of GDP, above the regional WAEMU ceiling. Non-performing loans passed 22 percent by mid-2025. Its resident representative warned that one-crop growth and falling labour productivity are not a base for lasting prosperity. [7] Offshore oil exploration was under way as of December 2025. [9]

The IMF completed the eleventh review of its Extended Credit Facility on 12 June, unlocking SDR 1.18 million. The programme totals SDR 38.59 million, and the Fund lists fuel prices, the cashew campaign and weather as risks. [29] WFP said on 1 June that nearly 130,000 people face crisis-level hunger in the lean season, that school-meal recipients fell from 283,400 to about 152,000, and that it needs 6.4 million dollars. [30] More than a quarter of people lived below the poverty line in 2023, according to the World Bank as cited by AFP. [8]

A US-funded hepatitis B vaccine trial planned by the Danish Bandim Health Project for about 14,000 babies was paused by the government in January. The WHO called it unethical in February, and judicial police raided Bandim's Bissau facilities in mid-October. The CDC had provided 1.6 million dollars. [31]

lenses.local: O Democrata quotes the PSTGB leader saying many low-paid school and state workers were not paid for the 2025/2026 school year, a claim from one party leader. [21]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera carried the vaccine-trial halt and AFP the poverty figure. [31][8]
lenses.scholar: The World Bank's update says firms lack the conditions that would let them expand and raise productivity. [7]

timeline.text: Embalo dissolves parliament after an armed clash he calls a coup attempt; parliament has not met since, AP reported in December 2025.
The government suspends RTP and Agencia Lusa and expels their journalists, according to GI-TOC.
The army announces an alleged coup plot, according to the Guinean Human Rights League as relayed by one outlet.
Presidential and legislative elections are held; Embalo and Dias both claim victory.
Officers announce a takeover a day before provisional results were due.
Maj.-Gen. Horta Inta-a is sworn in as transitional president for one year.
The military publishes a transitional charter barring the interim president and prime minister from standing.
ECOWAS rejects the transition plan and warns of targeted sanctions.
Inta-a announces presidential and legislative elections for 6 December 2026.
The body of youth movement leader Vigario Luis Balanta is found.
Pereira is placed in preventive detention in a case over an alleged October 2025 coup plot.
The ECOWAS summit in Lungi names Senegal facilitator of the transition.
Voters approve a new constitution that expands presidential powers.
The military high command refuses Embalo permission to return and run.
The prime minister and the electoral commission say the 6 December vote cannot be held.
Senegal's foreign minister arrives in Bissau to discuss a new election date.
Restrictions ease to allow party meetings, announced 6 November; rallies and demonstrations stay banned.

scores.coverage_basis: AFP, Reuters and AP filed around the coup, the referendum and the October postponement, with little steady flow between them. [11][17][3] Lusa and RTP file regularly from Portugal and O Democrata publishes from Bissau. [5][1] Crisis Group and ACLED material could not be retrieved for this draft.

severity.basis: The sources read report no insurgency, but soldiers seized power in November 2025, the army reported a coup plot in October 2025, and a youth movement leader was reportedly beaten to death in March. [9][20][16]
WFP counts nearly 130,000 people at crisis-level hunger and cut school meals for over 130,000 children, and more than a quarter of people lived below the poverty line in 2023. [30][8]
The UN reports bans on demonstrations and press conferences and closed party offices, and RSF ranks the country 100th of 180. [16][18]
Public debt is 75.6 percent of GDP and non-performing loans passed 22 percent, though growth was about 5.8 percent in 2025 and inflation 0.9 percent. [7][29]

The election was postponed with no new date, a constitution expanding presidential power passed amid empty polling stations, and party activity stays restricted, with a partial easing from 24 November. [3][17][5]

parts.basis: This draft found no source on US, Chinese or Russian forces or deals. The US CDC funded the contested vaccine trial with 1.6 million dollars. [31]
Cashew exports drive growth and offshore oil exploration was under way, but no figure on a share of world trade was found. [29][9]
The UN calls the country a gateway for drugs bound for Europe, and this is one of nine coups in West and Central Africa since 2020. [8][17]
Reach beyond the border runs mainly through the cocaine route to Europe, and no diaspora or migration figures were retrieved. [8]
ECOWAS rejected the transition plan and threatened sanctions, yet Semafor argues that regional bodies react after coups and cannot monitor erosion between elections. [24][9]

summary: Guinea-Bissau matters beyond its borders mainly as a cocaine transit point and as a test of how ECOWAS handles a military transition that keeps slipping. [8][24] Its economy is small and cashew-dependent, and this draft found no source on great-power bases or arms deals. [29]
gi.up: Confirmed great-power basing or arms deals, a large cocaine seizure tied to officials, or a counter-coup that draws in regional forces.
gi.down: A credible election held under an agreed timetable with ECOWAS and opposition buy-in.

gaps: Bissau Digital and Radio Sol Mansi did not surface in searches and were not read; local sourcing rests on three O Democrata articles read in Portuguese, so local coverage of the economy, the south and the islands is thin.
DW Portuguese and RFI were searched but no article from either was opened; the RFI-restricted search returned an error.

No page from state-run RDN, Radio Nacional or ANG was read or cited. RSF describes the state broadcaster, national radio, the No Pintcha newspaper and the state press agency as under strong government influence, but its page does not use the acronyms RDN or ANG. Any such source would carry the state_affiliated flag.

Crisis Group and ACLED: the Crisis Group country page and CrisisWatch pages failed to load or showed older material, and the ACLED country page held no data, so neither is cited. The only ISS item found is from 2014.
No fresh GI-TOC piece on 2026 trafficking was found; the drug section rests on GI-TOC's August 2025 report, AFP and AP. No 2026 seizure figures were found.
No source on US, Chinese, Russian or Gulf stakes was read, so the great-power score is low by default.
Embalo's location is reported differently: Al Jazeera and AP say the Republic of Congo, AFP says Morocco.
The charter is dated 4 December by International IDEA and 5 December by the UN Secretary-General's report; the page says early December. The UN report was read through a summary, not the full text.
The Transition Council adopted a constitution on 13 January per the UN, but the 30 August referendum is not mentioned in that report; the sequence between the two was not reconciled.
The 31 October 2025 alleged coup plot and the five detainees rest on one outlet relaying the Human Rights League; The Rio Times says its newsroom is automated.
The AFP referendum report says polling stations were largely empty, which conflicts with the official turnout of almost 60 percent; no independent turnout count was found.
Xinhua is state-affiliated and is used only for the Senegal facilitation appointment.
No new election date existed as of 25 November; a decree could arrive at any time. The Lusa report is dated 22 November.
No podcast or documentary on Guinea-Bissau was verified. The fact-check list is short.

reporters.name: Carolina Djeme
reporters.bio: Signs the 9 October 2026 O Democrata report on the Transition Council's opinion that a December vote is impossible.
reporters.why: Her report gives the council's own wording and spokesperson, which wires do not carry.
reporters.label: O Democrata GB

reporters.name: Assana Sambu
reporters.bio: Wrote the 25 October 2026 O Democrata report on the Senegalese minister's visit and the pending decree on a new election date.
reporters.why: The report lists whom the ECOWAS mediator planned to meet, including parties the wires skip.
reporters.label: O Democrata GB

reporters.name: Lucie Peytermann
reporters.bio: Bylined the 29 November 2025 AFP report on how the drug trade fuels instability after the coup.
reporters.why: The piece collects the junta's drug-plot claim, UN and GI-TOC findings and past prosecutions in one place.
reporters.label: eNCA (AFP)

reporters.name: Tomi Oladipo
reporters.bio: Wrote the 1 December 2025 Semafor analysis of the coup's timing and what it means for ECOWAS.
reporters.why: The analysis sets the coup against the Sahel coups and questions the regional response.
reporters.label: Semafor

reporters.name: Shola Lawal
reporters.bio: Wrote the 5 November 2026 Al Jazeera explainer on why Guinea-Bissau halted a US-funded hepatitis B vaccine trial.
reporters.why: A detailed account of the trial, the WHO objection and the October raid on Bandim.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Beverly Ochieng
reporters.bio: Quoted by AP in December 2025 saying one coup leader was Embalo's personal military adviser and that the takeover looks like an effort to preserve the status quo.
reporters.why: Her reading is one of the few named analyst views on whether the coup was staged.
reporters.label: AP (via Washington Times)

reporters.name: Lucia Bird
reporters.bio: Co-author with A. Gomes of the 4 February 2022 GI-TOC analysis of a reported coup attempt in Bissau.
reporters.why: The analysis ties the country's cycles of instability to the cocaine trade and cautions on official accounts.
reporters.label: GI-TOC

books.why: Examines the coups since 1998 and the country's rise as a drug-trafficking state, with chapters on history and social effects.

books.author: Ricardo Real P. de Sousa, Jens Herpolsheimer and Jara Cuadrado (eds)
books.why: Thirteen chapters on why the country stays unstable despite extensive international interventions, tied to regional and transnational dynamics.
